rationale: A wins because it treats the relaunch as a set of reportable tensions with scoreboards, not as a slogan machine. Its line, "the company has made a claim the next disclosure will settle," is exactly the kind of clean business-story frame a reporter can take to an editor. B has usable bones, but "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" is a headline wearing a fake mustache; the supplied facts prove Bumble launched AI, not that the category tipped.
gaps_in_A: "the first substantive product move since the founder's return this year" is not supplied. The update says the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is her first substantive move.
"Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating" overstates both sides: the facts give one company and "some users," not dating apps plural or users broadly.

"a relaunch built to reverse a decline" assumes company intent. The update says the relaunch follows declining paying users and a falling stock price; it does not say Bumble framed it as a reversal plan.
gaps_in_B: "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" is invented. One public company's relaunch is not enough to claim mainstream adoption or category-standard behavior.
"the relaunch is the company's public answer to the falling stock price and user decline" assigns motive the update does not provide.

"Bumble's brand promise is that its message-first model empowers authentic connection" decorates the supplied fact with mush. The facts say women-message-first remains core; they do not supply that brand-language wrapper.
"business or leadership reporter" and "tech-culture or dating-industry reporter" are too broad. That is not journalist shape; that is an address label.
